issues.item: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: This strategy is socially anxious/interpersonal in content and is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by war-zone danger cues, hypervigilant threat monitoring, and trauma-memory reactivation. The other strategies and threat/memory items coherently reflect trauma-related safety management, but rehearsing conversations before any interaction targets a different problem domain that is not represented elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, or Memory. Given the formulation, maladaptive strategies should plausibly feed back into triggers/threat/memory; this item does not connect well to those active nodes.

vignette:
Ethan was 29, a North American Jewish man who lived alone and worked as a jeweler in a small storefront district, the kind of job that required him to spend long hours bent over a counter under bright lights, handling tools and inspecting fine details. He had gone overseas as a relief worker into a war zone, telling people at the time that he could tolerate the chaos because he was useful there, because someone had to sort supplies, carry water, and help get children and families to safer ground. The day that changed him came when he was moving through a damaged school building that had been turned into a shelter. In the crush of bodies and shouting, he suddenly heard children crying from a back room, saw men carrying long metal objects that could have been tools or weapons, and felt an unexpected hand clamp onto his shoulder as someone tried to pull him aside. At the same instant, his own heart began pounding so hard that he could feel it in his throat. Since then, Ethan has said that even the smallest cue can drop him back into that moment without warning: the slam of a door near his apartment, a child wailing on the sidewalk, or the jolt of his pulse during an ordinary walk to work can bring the whole scene back with a force that feels immediate and overwhelming. He does not experience these memories as distant recollections. When one of those cues hits, it does not stay a cue for long; the sound or sensation itself seems to drag him straight back into the damaged school, and the memory arrives as if it is happening again rather than being remembered. He describes them as more real than his everyday life, vivid in their sounds and bodily sensations, and at times he feels the emotional intensity of the event flood him without any clear image at all, as if terror arrives first and the picture follows, if it follows at all. Because the memory comes back so vividly, he starts noticing reminders everywhere — a child crying outside the storefront, a hard jolt in his chest, a stranger’s hand near his shoulder — and each one gets read as another sign that the event is close behind him.

What has made those intrusions so hard to escape is the way Ethan now watches the world. Since returning home, he has been on constant alert for potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, and he cannot settle unless his back is against a wall where he can see the room. Even when friends or coworkers tell him he is safe, he finds it impossible to believe them. Living at that pitch of threat keeps the school memory active in his mind; the more dangerous the world feels, the more readily the scene returns, as though his body has to keep revisiting it to stay prepared for what might happen next. In his mind, safety is something other people can afford to assume, not something he is allowed to trust. That vigilance has made ordinary places feel full of hidden threat, and it also keeps the war zone memory close at hand, because every knife on a restaurant table, every heavy tool in the jewelry shop, every sudden movement near him seems to confirm that danger can appear anywhere. Once he is in that threat state, almost anything can turn into a reminder — the metal edges of a ring tray, a customer shifting too quickly at the counter, a door opening behind him — and the world around him starts to look arranged around the event. When he is scanning for threats, small physical sensations become loaded too. If his heart starts racing while he is leaning over a display case, he notices it instantly, and that pounding body sensation can pull the entire memory back into the room with him. Likewise, the sound of children crying outside the storefront or in the apartments above his shop can do the same. It does not matter that he knows he is in his own neighborhood; the fear in his body makes the past feel present.

Ethan has tried hard to manage this by talking himself down. He reminds himself that it could have been worse, that other people had it far worse, and he forces himself to think only positive thoughts when the images or feelings rise up. He tells himself to be grateful that he made it home, that he has work, that he is not in a bombed-out school anymore. But the effort of pushing it away has not emptied it out; keeping himself from thinking about it has only left the memory intact and waiting, so that when his guard slips the scene comes back louder and more forceful than before. But these efforts have not given him relief for long. Instead, they often seem to push the memory sideways rather than away, leaving him with the same violent emotional charge and, paradoxically, more scanning. When he tells himself to stay positive, he becomes even more determined not to look at what is wrong, and then the memory returns with its full force in some stray detail—a child’s cry, a shoulder brush from a stranger, his own pulse thudding in his chest. At those moments he begins checking the surroundings all over again, reading every corner of the room for danger, and the more he searches, the more dangerous the world appears. The habits built out of trying to manage his fear have also drawn a map of reminders around him, so that every route he avoids in the neighborhood, every place he chooses not to stand in the shop, and every hand he keeps at arm’s length becomes its own signal that the attack still matters. The shop has become especially difficult because he cannot control where customers stand or where their hands move, and an unexpected touch from behind the counter can make him jump hard enough that he has embarrassed himself in front of clients. Over time he has started choosing positions in the shop and in restaurants that let him keep his back protected, and he has cut short social outings because he cannot relax enough to stay.

The cost has been growing. Ethan has become quieter with friends, less willing to meet people after work, and increasingly isolated in his apartment, where he still finds himself scanning the rooms before he can sit down. His days are organized around not being startled, not being cornered, not hearing children cry if he can help it. He finally sought help after a morning in the shop when his heart began racing as a parent and child passed outside, the child crying against the glass while a customer touched his arm from behind to ask a question. The memory hit him so fully that he had to step into the back room and sit on the floor until he could breathe. He came to treatment afraid that his body and mind were no longer obeying him, and most afraid that he would keep living as if the war were still happening, unable to trust that he is truly home.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows cues bringing back the memory, but does not clearly state that triggers themselves cause or lead to the traumatic memory in the same-paragraph causal sense required.
The vignette describes the memory leading Ethan to scan for cues, but it does not clearly state that the memory itself generates or activates triggers/reminders.
The vignette portrays Ethan as perceiving the world as dangerous, but it does not explicitly connect that sense of threat to the traumatic memory coming back.
The vignette shows that threat scanning happens alongside reminders of danger, but it does not clearly say that his sense of threat causes specific triggers/reminders to arise.
Ethan uses talking himself down and positive thinking, but the vignette does not clearly state that these maladaptive strategies lead to the memory returning or being maintained.
The vignette shows his coping efforts alongside later checking and scanning, but it does not clearly state that the maladaptive strategies themselves generate triggers/reminders.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette shows cues bringing back the memory, but does not clearly state that triggers themselves cause or lead to the traumatic memory in the same-paragraph causal sense required.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette describes the memory leading Ethan to scan for cues, but it does not clearly state that the memory itself generates or activates triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette portrays Ethan as perceiving the world as dangerous, but it does not explicitly connect that sense of threat to the traumatic memory coming back.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette shows that threat scanning happens alongside reminders of danger, but it does not clearly say that his sense of threat causes specific triggers/reminders to arise.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: Ethan uses talking himself down and positive thinking, but the vignette does not clearly state that these maladaptive strategies lead to the memory returning or being maintained.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette shows his coping efforts alongside later checking and scanning, but it does not clearly state that the maladaptive strategies themselves generate triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
